subChunks.title: Internal Platforms, Developer Experience & Golden Paths
subChunks.hookHtml: As engineering organisations grow, teams repeatedly solve the same infrastructure problems — CI pipelines, deployment tooling, service scaffolding, observability setup. Platform thinking recognises that this is waste, and that investing in shared internal tooling can multiply the productivity of every engineering team that uses it. But platform engineering done badly creates a burden rather than a capability.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Platform Engineering Is

Platform engineering builds and maintains internal capabilities that product engineering teams consume as a service. The platform team's customer is other engineers, not end users. Common platform products: CI/CD infrastructure, service scaffolding and templates, internal developer portal, observability tooling, authentication libraries, deployment tooling.

The measure of a platform's success is the reduction in toil for the teams that use it — not the sophistication of the platform itself.

The Golden Path

A Golden Path is the recommended, well-maintained way to do something within the organisation. It is not mandatory — but it is the path of least resistance, and it comes with tooling, documentation, and support. Teams that follow the Golden Path get: quick setup, known-good configuration, automatic updates, and support from the platform team. Teams that diverge take on the maintenance burden themselves.

Golden Paths for common needs: 'start a new Java microservice', 'add a new CI pipeline', 'set up structured logging', 'deploy to Cloud Run'. Each path is a documented, templated, automated flow that embodies the organisation's best practices.

Internal Developer Portal (IDP)

A central interface for engineers to discover platform capabilities, provision resources (create a new service, get a database), and understand system inventory. Backstage (by Spotify) is the most common open-source foundation. An IDP reduces the 'how do I even start?' friction that new engineers face and prevents the slow drift of undocumented services.

The Product Mindset for Platform Teams

Platform teams must treat engineering teams as customers with a product mindset — not as internal stakeholders to be accommodated. This means: understanding the 'jobs to be done' by the teams they serve, measuring adoption and customer satisfaction (developer NPS, time-to-first-service, deployment frequency), prioritising based on impact rather than technical interest, and deprecating platforms that teams are not using.

Platform teams that build tools engineers don't want, or that build tools correctly but document them poorly, fail even if the technology is excellent.

Avoiding Platform Over-Engineering

Platform teams can fall into the trap of building impressive infrastructure for its own sake. Signs: the platform has many features but low adoption, platform teams spend more time on the platform than on the product teams' problems, or no one except the platform team understands how to use it. The corrective: apply the same build-vs-buy discipline to platform decisions. If a managed cloud service does 90% of what an internal platform would do, the internal platform must deliver clearly more value to justify the build cost.

storyBeats.text: The Academy grew from 5 to 50 engineers over three years. Each new engineer spent their first two weeks figuring out how to set up a development environment, how to deploy code, and how to add monitoring. Four different teams had built four different ways to do each of these things. A fifth of the time of every new hire was spent on infrastructure archaeology. The platform team's first product took that two weeks down to one day.

storyBeats.speaker: Platform Lead Osta
storyBeats.text: Platform engineering only matters if the product teams actually use the platform. I have seen platform teams build beautiful internal Kubernetes operators that nobody adopted. The measure is not technical quality — it is the reduction in toil for the teams we serve. If engineers still copy-paste their CI config from the team Slack rather than using the template we provide, the template has failed regardless of how elegant it is.

storyBeats.speaker: Platform Lead Osta
storyBeats.text: The Golden Path is not a mandate. If you make it mandatory, teams route around it and build resentment. If you make it the easiest path — the path with the template, the docs, the examples, the on-call support — teams adopt it because it saves them time. The Golden Path succeeds through convenience, not compulsion.

storyBeats.speaker: Platform Lead Osta
storyBeats.text: Before building any platform tool, interview five engineers from product teams. Ask: what takes you the most time? What do you wish was already done for you? What documentation do you most often re-read? The answers are your platform roadmap. Build based on the highest-frequency pain points, not on what is technically interesting to the platform team.

learningObjectives: Define platform engineering and explain how the measure of success differs from product engineering
Describe the Golden Path concept and explain why it should be adopted through convenience rather than mandate
Identify the components of an effective Internal Developer Portal
Apply the product mindset to a platform team's prioritisation decisions
commonMistakes: Building platform tooling without interviewing the engineers it is meant to serve
Making the Golden Path mandatory rather than the easiest option — creates resistance and workarounds
Measuring platform success by feature count rather than engineer adoption and toil reduction
Building an internal platform when a managed cloud service would deliver 90% of the value with no maintenance burden
assessmentCriteria: Can articulate what a Golden Path is and describe two specific Golden Path examples for a Java engineering org
Can describe how to measure a platform's success in terms of developer outcomes rather than platform features
Can apply the product mindset to prioritise three platform investments based on impact, effort, and adoption likelihood
Can identify the build-vs-buy decision for a platform capability and justify the recommendation
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain platform engineering to a senior engineer who thinks it means 'the team that builds internal tools nobody uses.' What is a Golden Path? What does developer experience actually mean in practice? How do you measure whether a platform is succeeding?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following platform engineering questions:

  1. You are the platform lead at the Academy (50 engineers, 10 product teams). You conduct interviews and find the top three pain points: (a) setting up a new service takes 3 days of manual steps, (b) no standard way to add structured logging — each team has a different configuration, (c) deployment requires knowledge of 12 different CLI flags. Design one Golden Path for each pain point.
  2. Your platform team built an internal Kubernetes dashboard 6 months ago. Adoption is 15% (3 of 20 eligible teams). What questions would you ask to diagnose the problem, and what are the likely causes?
  3. Should you build an internal secrets management platform or use GCP Secret Manager? Apply the build-vs-buy framework.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Three Golden Paths:

   (a) New service creation — currently 3 days of manual steps:
   Golden Path: a CLI scaffold (e.g. 'academy-cli new-service spell-search') that generates:
   - A Spring Boot project with standard dependencies pre-wired (SLF4J, Micrometer, Spring Security JWT)
   - A CI/CD pipeline file (GitHub Actions) with build/test/deploy stages
   - A Dockerfile following the layered build pattern
   - A Cloud Run deployment config with standard resource limits
   - A README with team ownership, port, and health endpoint documented
   Result: first deployment in 4 hours instead of 3 days. Template is maintained by platform team.

   (b) Structured logging — each team different:
   Golden Path: publish a shared logging library (academy-logging-starter) as a Maven BOM dependency:
   - Configures Logback JSON layout automatically
   - Provides MDC utilities (withCorrelationId(), withUserId())
   - Includes a Spring filter that adds X-Request-Id to MDC on each request
   Documentation: one-page 'add logging to your service in 5 minutes.'
   Teams that include the starter get correct logging. Teams that don't are flagged in the architecture scan.

   (c) Deployment with 12 CLI flags:
   Golden Path: a deployment script ('academy-deploy spell-service production') that encapsulates all flags with environment-specific defaults. Engineers specify service name and environment; the script handles the rest. Override flags available but not required.

2. 15% adoption of Kubernetes dashboard:
   Questions to ask:
   - Did we ask product teams what they actually need before building this?
   - Where do engineers currently go to get this information (existing solution)?
   - What does the onboarding experience look like — can an engineer use it in under 5 minutes?
   - Have we asked the 85% who aren't using it why not?
   Likely causes:
   - Teams don't need a Kubernetes view — they deploy to Cloud Run (not K8s) and see what they need in GCP console
   - Discovery problem: teams don't know it exists, or how to log in, or what it shows them
   - Too complex: shows infrastructure detail that product engineers don't care about
   Action: run 3 user interviews with non-adopters. If the need isn't there, deprecate and redirect resources.

3. Build internal secrets management vs GCP Secret Manager:
   GCP Secret Manager provides: encrypted storage, fine-grained IAM, audit logging, automatic rotation, Cloud Run integration, 100% availability SLA.
   Building internally provides: custom UI, organisation-specific workflow, no vendor dependency.
   Decision: use GCP Secret Manager. The managed service provides 95%+ of what an internal build would achieve, with none of the operational burden. An internal secrets management platform is security-critical — the blast radius of a bug is high. Platform team time is better spent on the highest-friction engineer pain points (see above). ADR written: 'Use GCP Secret Manager; revisit if multi-cloud strategy requires vendor-neutral secrets management.'
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Design a minimal Internal Developer Portal for the Academy. The Academy has 50 engineers, 20 services, 4 product teams, and no current centralised way to discover service ownership, API contracts, or runbooks. Answer: (1) What are the core capabilities the portal must have on day 1 (minimum viable portal)? (2) What data does it surface and how does it stay up to date? (3) How do you measure whether engineers are actually using it? (4) What is the biggest risk to adoption and how do you mitigate it?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. Minimum viable portal (day 1):
   - Service catalogue: list of all 20 services with owner team, on-call contact, source repo link, and environment URLs
   - API docs: link to each service's OpenAPI spec (auto-generated from Spring endpoints)
   - Runbook links: one runbook URL per service (can start as a wiki page)
   - New service wizard: the scaffold Golden Path from a UI (click through, download generated project)
   What NOT to build on day 1: complex dependency graphs, custom metrics dashboards, ticket integration — add only when adoption justifies the investment.

2. Data and freshness:
   Service catalogue: populated from a YAML file in each service's repo (backstage-style catalog-info.yaml). Changes merged to main → portal updates within minutes via webhook. Staleness is caught by a weekly CI check that reports missing/outdated catalog files.
   API docs: auto-generated from the service's running OpenAPI endpoint on each deployment (CI step pushes spec to portal).
   Runbooks: team-maintained; staleness tracked by last-edited date surfaced in the portal.

3. Measuring adoption:
   - Active users per week (portal analytics)
   - Service catalogue completeness: % of services with all required fields filled
   - New engineer onboarding time to first successful deployment (survey after first 30 days)
   - Search query log: what are engineers searching for and not finding? (highest-value backlog input)
   Success metric: 80% of engineers visit the portal at least once per week by month 3.

4. Biggest adoption risk and mitigation:
   Risk: engineers already have their own way of finding this information (Slack, shared docs, memory) and the portal adds friction rather than removing it.
   Mitigation:
   - Make the portal the canonical source that Slack searches recommend ('for service owners, see the portal')
   - Remove the competing sources (archive the old service list wiki after migration)
   - Ensure the portal is faster than the alternative — if it takes 5 clicks to find a runbook but Slack search takes 10 seconds, the portal loses
   - First-week onboarding for new engineers explicitly includes 'find service X in the portal' as an exercise

questions.questionHtml: What is a 'Golden Path' in the context of platform engineering?
options: A mandatory standard that all teams must follow
The recommended, well-maintained, templated way to accomplish a common task — adopted through convenience, not mandate
A senior engineer's approved solution pattern
questions.correctAnswer: The recommended, well-maintained, templated way to accomplish a common task — adopted through convenience, not mandate
questions.explanationHtml: A Golden Path is the path of least resistance for a common engineering task — building a service, adding CI, setting up logging. It comes with templates, documentation, and support, making it faster and easier than building from scratch. It is not mandatory; teams can deviate, but then take on full maintenance responsibility. Adoption through convenience outperforms adoption through enforcement — mandate creates resentment and workarounds.

questions.questionHtml: A platform team built a sophisticated internal observability platform with 20 features. Only 2 of 15 product teams use it. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The platform team built what was technically interesting rather than what product teams actually needed
The platform needs more features before it's useful
Product teams need to be mandated to use it
questions.correctAnswer: The platform team built what was technically interesting rather than what product teams actually needed
questions.explanationHtml: Low adoption despite high feature count is the classic signal of building without customer research. Platform teams that don't regularly interview the engineers they serve tend to optimise for technical elegance rather than solving the actual highest-friction pain points. The fix: cancel the next feature, run five user interviews with non-adopters, and rebuild the roadmap around what those engineers actually need — which is almost certainly simpler than what was built.

questions.questionHtml: A platform team's primary success metric should be the number of features their internal platform offers.
questions.explanationHtml: Platform success is measured by outcomes for the teams that use it: reduction in toil, time-to-first-deployment, adoption rate, developer NPS, deployment frequency. A platform with 20 features that 2 teams use has failed. A platform with 3 features that reduces new service setup from 3 days to 4 hours and is adopted by 90% of teams has succeeded. Feature count is a vanity metric for platform teams — customer outcome is the measure.
